items.title: Leading a team to the end
items.body: Led planning through scheduling as team lead 4 times. On CapTeam I designed the student and admin screen structure as team lead and owned the frontend on my own; the team won the school capstone project grand prize.

items.title: Beyond the screen, into operations
items.body: Repeated API calls are not only a speed problem — they add load on the server. I checked in the Network tab where calls piled up and cut the number of calls. I keep a record of what the frontend can solve and what needs a backend change.

items.title: Verifying after using AI
items.body: I check what AI produces on the screen, Network, E2E and mobile viewports. Code being written and code working in the real service are two different things.

TechStack.title: Tech Stack
TechStack.headline:
I pick the tool the work calls for,
and record where and why I used it
TechStack.note: Each entry carries the context in which I actually used it.

desc.react: Split screens into components and reused repeated UI behind a defined interface. Organised the states a screen can hold — inputs, modals, loading, errors — with useState, and moved flows outside the screen into custom hooks so components stay focused on rendering.
desc.javascript: Write on ES6+ syntax. Shape server responses to the screen's structure with map, filter, find and slice, and handle async flows with async/await and Promises. Design the failure path alongside the happy path with try/catch/finally, so a failed request never leaves the user with an empty screen.
desc.reactRouter: Used the URL as the unit of a screen, splitting routes and separating detail views with dynamic parameters. Controlled navigation from code as well as from links, so a screen could hand off once its work was done.
desc.zustand: Managed auth state and the login session in a global store, shared across screens. Kept the state outside the component tree so screens read it directly without passing props, and paired it with a custom hook to keep call sites simple.
desc.axios: Owned communication with the backend API. Checked in the Network tab where repeated calls piled up and reduced the number of calls. Recorded what the frontend could solve and what required a backend change.
desc.cssModules: Isolate styles per component so class names never collide. Colour, spacing and typography live as CSS variables in one place, and light and dark themes swap behind the same variable names.
desc.nextjs: Learning the App Router and server component model — where to place the boundary between rendering and data fetching, and how far the code shipped in the client bundle can be reduced.
desc.typescript: Learning to catch errors before runtime with types: defining a function's input and output first, and making the points where a value may be absent visible in the type.
desc.tailwind: Learning utility-class styling, measured against the CSS Modules I use today: which approach stays easier to read and change as a project grows.

capteam.summary: A service that connects student survey data to AI team recommendations, lets admins review, adjust, and approve the results, and carries them through to team operations.

capteam.problem: Surveys alone could not reflect a student's role, skill level and project experience at once. Even after the teams were set, notices, logs, plans and chat lived in separate places, so there was no way to see progress at a glance.
approach: Feed survey data into AI team recommendations
Let an admin review the reasoning, swap members and approve
Connect the confirmed team and its tools to the student screens
Bring notices, logs, project plans and chat into one flow

capteam.ai: The problem definition, service flow and screen design were my own work. In later implementation and maintenance I relied heavily on Codex, and checked what it produced in the browser, in Console and Network, and through builds, lint, E2E and mobile viewports.

troubleshooting.title: Duplicate AI team requests and lost progress on reload
troubleshooting.situation: AI team creation returned a job id and ran on the server. Pressing the button again or reloading could create a duplicate job or lose the progress.
troubleshooting.task: I had to identify a job once it started, so that re-entering the page could keep reading the state of the same jobId.
action: Stored the jobId right after the request
Locked the button and blocked re-requests while a job was running
Reflected progress, success and failure by polling on the jobId
Restored the saved job on reload and re-entry
outcome: Admins no longer lose track of progress

troubleshooting.title: Repeated API calls and rising server requests
troubleshooting.situation: E2E and Network logs showed dashboard, header, unread and channel summary requests repeating on every screen change and poll. The admin chat list also had an N+1 pattern.
troubleshooting.task: I had to cut unnecessary calls and concurrent duplicate requests while keeping the feature working.
action: A short TTL cache, with in-flight requests shared
Skipped unread polling in background tabs
Removed the duplicate read call when a channel is selected
Recorded that removing the N+1 pattern fully needs a batch API on the backend
outcome: Fewer repeated calls and edge requests
Clear split between frontend fixes and backend work

troubleshooting.title: UI and accessibility warnings found through E2E
troubleshooting.situation: Walking teacher and student flows at 390, 412 and 768px surfaced nested list items, duplicate React keys and horizontal overflow on mobile.
troubleshooting.task: I had to clear warnings that do not look like bugs, and verify the permission, empty and exception flows again.
action: Rewrote the notice list as ul → li → link
Applied React keys based on team and order
Checked wrong sign-in, protected routes, survey completion, log time guards and empty input validation
Re-checked horizontal overflow on mobile and Console warnings
outcome: Overflow and React warnings gone on the screens I tested
A verification pass covering access, empty states and exceptions

learned.title: Screens are not the whole job — data flow and the runtime environment matter
items: I learned that repeated calls are not just a speed problem — they add load on the server.
Wiring up polling myself, I found that a start condition is not enough — it needs a stop condition and a way to resume.
I came away with a basis for telling apart what the frontend can fix and what needs a backend API change.

learned.title: When you build with AI, verification is still yours
items: I saw for myself that code being written is not the same as it working in the real flow.
With features that carry state — JWT, polling, WebSocket — I got into the habit of following the data flow all the way through.
Even when I leaned on AI, I learned that defining the requirement and verifying the result stay with me.
